items.abstract: <jats:p>A learning management system (LMS) plays a crucial role in supporting students’ educational activities by centralized platforms for course delivery, communication, and student support. Recently, many universities have integrated chatbots into their LMS to assist students with various inquiries and tasks. However, existing chatbots often necessitate human interventions to manually respond to complex queries, resulting in limited scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we present a memory-augmented large language model (LLM) framework that enhances the reasoning and contextual continuity of LMS-based chatbots. The proposed framework first embeds user queries and retrieves semantically relevant entries from various LMS resources, including instructional documents and academic frequently asked questions. Retrieved entries are then filtered through a two-stage confidence filtering process that combines similarity thresholds and LLM-based semantic validation. Validated information, along with user queries, is processed by LLM for response generation. To maintain coherence in multi-turn interactions, the chatbot incorporates short-term, long-term, and temporal event memories, which track conversational flow and personalize responses based on user-specific information, such as recent activity history and individual preferences. To evaluate response quality, we employed a multi-layered evaluation strategy combining BERTScore-based quantitative measurement, an LLM-as-a-Judge approach for automated semantic assessment, and a user study under multi-turn scenarios. The evaluation results consistently confirm that the proposed framework improves the consistency, clarity, and usefulness of the responses. These findings highlight the potential of memory-augmented LLMs for scalable and intelligent learning support within university environments.</jats:p>
title: Memory-Augmented Large Language Model for Enhanced Chatbot Services in University Learning Management Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate across extended time horizons, yet their memory systems remain poorly suited to sustained, goal-directed tasks. Most existing approaches optimize for recall quality in isolation, neglecting the intertwined costs of latency, token consumption, and temporal coherence. We introduce the Weighted Developmental Memory Architecture (WDMA), a theoretical framework that models agent memory as a five-layer, salience-gated system governed by thermodynamic efficiency principles. WDMA introduces three core contributions: (1) a jolt-based encoding mechanism in which memories are formed proportional to prediction-error magnitude, with thresholds that co-evolve with domain competence; (2) a D0-D5 expansion taxonomy that classifies synthetic memory training data by semantic transformation depth, from raw replay to calibration signals; and (3) a promotion utility function U (m) that scores memory entries for layer advancement based on recency, novelty, correctness, and access cost. We further characterize three failure modes-self-confirmation loops, stale-memory contamination, and false causal attribution-and propose architectural mitigations for each. While empirical validation remains future work, WDMA provides a principled vocabulary and design space for researchers building the next generation of persistent, adaptive AI agents.</jats:p>
title: Weighted Developmental Memory Architecture (WDMA): A Theoretical Framework for Cost-Aware, Self-Evolving Memory Systems in Large Language Model Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>The deployment of large language models (LLMs) on memory-constrained devices remains a significant challenge in bringing advanced AI to consumer hardware. Existing approaches either accept severe quality degradation through model compression or require impractical hardware specifications. We present ADAPT (Adaptive Decomposition and Parallel Task Execution), a novel execution framework that enables efficient LLM inference on devices with as little as 4GB VRAM by intelligently decomposing queries into parallelizable micro-tasks and dynamically selecting among three distinct execution modes based on query complexity and system state. The core innovation of ADAPT is its tri-series execution strategy: Series 1 performs parallel GPU core allocation for complex queries, Series 2 implements fast CPU-GPU exchange for simple queries, and Series 3 adaptively switches between modes based on runtime metrics. Through query decomposition analysis, GPU core group allocation, and intelligent compilation of distributed results, ADAPT achieves 6x memory efficiency compared to baseline approaches while maintaining inference quality. We demonstrate that models with 30B parameters can execute effectively on consumer-grade hardware through selective module activation and INT4 quantization. Our evaluation shows Series 1 execution provides a 3.3x speedup for complex queries through parallelization, while Series 2 achieves sub-second latency for simple queries through lightweight CPU-GPU communication. ADAPT represents a paradigm shift from parameter-centric scaling to execution-centric optimization, making advanced AI practical for local deployment while maintaining safety and interpretability.</jats:p>
title: ADAPT: Adaptive Decomposition and Parallel Task Execution for Memory-Efficient Large Language Model Inference

items.abstract: <jats:p>Home Energy Management Systems (HEMSs) help households tailor their electricity usage based on power system signals such as energy prices. This technology helps to reduce energy bills and offers greater demand-side flexibility that supports the power system stability. However, residents who lack a technical background may find it difficult to use HEMSs effectively, because HEMSs require well-formatted parameterization that reflects the characteristics of the energy resources, houses, and users’ needs. Recently, Large-Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated an outstanding ability in language understanding. Motivated by this, we propose an LLM-based interface that interacts with users to understand and parameterize their “badly-formatted answers”, and then outputs well-formatted parameters to implement an HEMS. We further use Reason and Act method (ReAct) and few-shot prompting to enhance the LLM performance. Evaluating the interface performance requires multiple user–LLM interactions. To avoid the efforts in finding volunteer users and reduce the evaluation time, we additionally propose a method that uses another LLM to simulate users with varying expertise, ranging from knowledgeable to non-technical. By comprehensive evaluation, the proposed LLM-based HEMS interface achieves an average parameter retrieval accuracy of 88%, outperforming benchmark models without ReAct and/or few-shot prompting.</jats:p>
title: Large Language Model Interface for Home Energy Management Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being integrated into instruction-driven task planning within various external environments, such as games, compilers, and Application Programming Interfaces. Obtaining planning scenarios from Large Language Model(LLM) greatly mitigates the time and computational costs associated with rule-based and network-based approaches, but still suffers from limited contextual horizons and a lack of real-time cognitive and interactive capabilities with real environments. The engineering application point of this paper is: To address the challenges, we introduce a large language model-based task planning agent to facilitate human-computer interaction and application of LLMs in real-world task planning activities, which has a generative memory (GM-Agent) that responds to the textualized reality of planning events. The contribution in GM-Agent leverages the inherent rules and worldviews extracted from textual data, employing generative memory modules to assimilate planning knowledge from expert experiences. This framework has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in four out of five tasks set by LandWar, matching the performance of the Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback(RLHF) model in knowledge quiz tasks, despite having an equivalent number of parameters. Additionally, we have performed comprehensive comparison and ablation studies involving LLMs and various configurations, providing a detailed analysis of performance influencers and highlighting areas requiring further exploration.</jats:p>
title: Large Language Model-Based Planning Agent with Generative Memory Strengthens Performance in Textualized World

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in cloud environments presents significant challenges due to their substantial memory footprint and computational requirements. While serverless architectures offer attractive pay-per-use economics, they suffer from prohibitively long cold start times when loading multi-gigabyte model weights into GPU memory. This paper presents FlashServe, a serverless LLMinference system that achieves fast cold starts through three key innovations: (1) a tiered memory snapshotting mechanism that pre-stages model checkpoints in host DRAM and leverages high-speed DMAtransfers via PCIe for rapid GPU memory loading, (2) a hybrid Prophet-LSTM prediction model for proactive pod pre-warming based on request arrival patterns, and (3) efficient LoRA adapter multiplexing that enables serving multiple fine-tuned models on shared GPU resources. Extensive experiments on the Azure Functions trace dataset demonstrate that FlashServe reduces cold start latency by up to 49× compared to baseline S3-based loading approaches and by 3.3× compared to state-of-the-art systems like ServerlessLLM. Under realistic bursty workloads, FlashServe achieves 32% reduction in GPU idle costs while maintaining sub-second time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency for 95%of requests. These results demonstrate that FlashServe represents meaningful progress toward practical serverless LLM deployment.</jats:p>
title: FlashServe: Cost-Efficient Serverless Inference Scheduling for Large Language Models via Tiered Memory Management and Predictive Autoscaling

items.abstract: Symbolic memory residuals were introduced as phase-alternating, high-dimensional signals injected into transformer layers to explore latent modulation of gradient dynamics during LLM training. Without modifying architectural components or optimization objectives, the mechanism indirectly influenced convergence trajectories through synthetic phase structures detached from loss gradients. Oscillatory injection schedules produced measurable variations in activation energy, attention entropy, and layer normalization behavior, reflecting nontrivial interaction between symbolic rhythm and representational evolution. Residual symbolic vectors projected orthogonally to token embeddings induced alignment-dependent variance in hidden state propagation, yielding periodic reweighting of gradient contributions across layers. Comparative evaluations against control configurations highlighted non-monotonic differences in token retention patterns, inter-layer embedding coherence, and sparsity in parameter updates. Symbolic phase transitions generated structured activation perturbations that reshaped internal state flows without requiring any learned supervision or architectural augmentation. The results indicate that phase-aligned symbolic injection introduces a lightweight, architecture-agnostic mechanism for exploring structured modulation of internal behavior during LLM training. Broader implications may extend to training regimes that benefit from implicit regularization or controlled activation cycling, although theoretical formalization remains an open question.
title: Latent Phase Alternation Through Symbolic Memory Residuals in Large Language Model Gradient Reweighting

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of Large Language Models into recommender systems has unlocked new potential in cognitive semantic reasoning and user understanding. However, the efficacy of existing LLM-based approaches in capturing long-term and evolving user preferences is constrained by finite context windows and the lack of structured knowledge representation mechanisms. Prevalent methods typically rely on flat or monolithic memory structures, which suffer from noise accumulation and fail to effectively disentangle transient short-term intents from enduring long-term preferences, particularly within dynamic conversational environments.To address these limitations, we reconceptualize LLM-based recommendation as a hierarchical knowledge modeling problem, positing that user preference evolution requires structured cognitive abstraction rather than mere information storage. To this end, we propose the Hierarchical ContextAware Memory System (HCAMS), a framework that organizes user knowledge into three granularity levels: an Instance Memory Tier (IMT) for preserving episodic behavioral details, a Semantic Aggregation Tier (SAT) for abstracting high-level preference schemas, and a Context-Aware Adaptation Tier (CAAT) that functions as a control policy to regulate memory access based on real-time contextual signals.Distinguishing itself from methods that treat context as auxiliary features, HCAMS utilizes context as an active gating mechanism that governs the access to different knowledge granularities. This hierarchical design enables the system to balance short-term responsiveness with long-term preference stability, while improving robustness against preference drift and contextual volatility. By integrating HCAMS with an LLM, the proposed framework effectively decouples memory retention from reasoning, allowing the LLM to perform grounded semantic inference over structured evidence rather than noisy raw sequences.</jats:p>
title: Hierarchical Context-Aware Dynamic Memory System for Large Language Model Recommendation with evolving user interests

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large-scale Transformer-based language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and GPT-4 require substantial memory resources, with GPT-3's 175 billion parameters demanding approximately 356 GB at 16-bit precision. This memory burden stems from dense weight matrices, linearly-growing key-value (KV) caches, and redundant knowledge re-encoding across inference cycles. We introduce the Persistent Memory Logic Loop (PMLL), a novel architecture that augments standard Transformers with an external, compressed persistent memory pool, queue-theoretic promise semantics, and recursive compression algorithms. PMLL achieves a 59-60% reduction in memory footprint while maintaining accuracy within 1.5% of baseline models. Our approach combines modular placement using collision-free hash functions, importance-weighted pruning, vector quantization, and memory-efficient attention mechanisms. Experimental validation on WikiText-2, PG-19, and OpenWebText datasets demonstrates consistent performance gains. Additionally, we present a novel Fourier-Hypotenuse Path Refinement algorithm for the Traveling Salesman Problem that achieves within 1.5% of optimal solutions using O(N) memory. This work provides both theoretical foundations and production-ready implementations for deploying memory-efficient LLMs at scale.</jats:p>
title: Persistent Memory Logic Loop (PMLL) Architecture: Memory Footprint Reduction in Large Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper examines whether decisions generated by large language model (LLM) agents can be represented by simple equations in an agent-based model of bank balance-sheet management. In a monthly leader-follower model, a stylised, predominantly deposit-funded euro-area bank chooses deposit rates, lending margins and the composition of bond reinvestment, while depositors and borrowers respond to these decisions and to economic conditions. The initial balance sheet is calibrated to selected indicators from regulatory disclosures. We estimate equation-based approximations of LLM-generated decisions and evaluate them against simulations not used in estimation. Across ten out-of-sample bank-year simulations, the final specification reproduces annual return on equity (ROE) within 0.31 percentage points and meets all fit criteria in seven; none of the deposit-run scenarios meets all criteria. In eighteen simulations with a second LLM family, the ROE difference does not exceed 0.71 percentage points, but only six meet all criteria. Against a market-pricing rule, the original optimisation model, and regression and nearest-neighbour approximations estimated on the same data, the final specification meets all criteria in more years and tracks liquidity most closely in deposit-run years. Instructions without behavioural guidance show that withdrawal magnitudes and fixed-rate borrowers' price sensitivity depend materially on the instructions supplied; with customer equations estimated under neutral instructions, a two-month withdrawal episode no longer becomes self-sustaining. The results demonstrate a procedure for approximating and evaluating LLM-generated decisions within a defined simulation environment; they do not establish that these responses represent the behaviour of bank managers or customers. AI-use disclosure: Large language models are used as simulated decision-making agents in this study. Separately, Claude assisted with simulation-code development, bibliographic checking and editorial consistency, and ChatGPT assisted with manuscript editing and condensation. The author is responsible for the research design, analyses, interpretation and final text.</jats:p>
title: Estimating Decision Rules from Large Language Model Agents: An Application to Bank Balance-Sheet Management

items.abstract: <jats:p>Access Control Management (ACM) is a fundamental security measure of information systems, governing which resources a user can access and under what conditions. Typically, effective ACM requires significant manual effort for policy specification, enforcement, and maintenance. To alleviate this burden, prior research has explored automating ACM by integrating machine learning solutions. However, the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and, more recently, LLM agents has opened up many new challenges and opportunities for information systems. Although a plethora of studies currently focus on LLM security, they primarily address adversarial threats, leaving the specific implications for ACM largely underexplored. In this article, we address this gap by surveying the synergistic integration of ACM and LLM agents from a twofold perspective: agents for ACM, where agents assist security administrators in automating the management of access control; and ACM for agents, where access control principles are applied to regulate the behavior, permissions, and security boundaries of the agents themselves. Through these two lenses, we disentangle and define three core ACM tasks, which are receiving increasing attention but are not yet clearly defined in the literature: access control policy generation, decision-making, and enforcement. Furthermore, we conceptualize agents as three core components of standard access-control models: agents as Subjects, Objects, and Actions. To survey existing solutions, we formalize the interaction flow between users and agents and categorize four restriction mechanisms for ACM: user authentication, agent customization, LLM customization, and tools. Building on these mechanisms, we provide a critical analysis of the state-of-the-art, and finally outline open challenges and future research directions to foster stronger cohesion between ACM and LLM agents.</jats:p>
title: The Synergistic Integration of Access Control Management and Large Language Model Agents: A Survey

items.abstract: <jats:p>This research incorporates artificial intelligence (AI) into asset integrity and process safety (AIPS) management, aiming to revolutionize conventional methods. It facilitates the automation of risk assessments, enhances predictive analytics, and supports the development of proactive measures to mitigate potential incidents. It explores the application of a generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) based large language models (LLM) to analyse and classify AIPS indicators from vast datasets to generate actionable recommendations to prevent future incidents. A comparative study between two onshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants; one utilizing AI-driven AIPS management and the other relying on manual data analysis is presented. The results indicate that AI-driven approaches significantly enhance the accuracy and speed of incident classifications, reducing data processing times. The test model effectively predicts potential future failures by analysing past incident patterns, enabling informed decision-making to prevent and mitigate future failures. The findings highlight the importance of adopting AI-driven AIPS management as a standard practice. It also emphasises the need for stronger collaboration between academia and industry in AI solutions to drive technological advancements for sustainability.</jats:p>
title: An Industrial Application of a Large Language Model to Enhancing Asset Integrity and Process Safety Management

items.abstract: <jats:p>Selective machine unlearning aims to suppress targeted information while preserving retained and general knowledge. We investigate valence-aware gradient memory within low-rank adaptation (LoRA), separating retention-supporting and forgetting-related directions. Earlier experiments used Gamma-scaled exponential moving averages rather than genuine fractional dynamics; we preserve that distinction and introduce a normalized finite-history Grünwald–Letnikov (GL) fractional-integral accumulator with algebraically decaying coefficients. The study progresses from synthetic transformer optimization and pretrained text classification to causal language model experiments, including a new controlled evaluation on TOFU Forget10 using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. A SciQ- and WikiText-regularized teacher reduces reference-answer NLL on original and paraphrased TOFU questions while exhibiting a small World Facts penalty in a separate audit. From this fixed teacher, four unlearning methods were compared for 120 updates over three random seeds. Dual GL yields the largest paraphrased forget-set NLL increase (2.169±0.331), exceeding dual EMA (1.964±0.250), but incurs greater retain-set (1.043±0.207 versus 0.914±0.147) and World Facts (1.333±0.645 versus 1.153±0.567) degradation. Exact paired sign-flip tests do not establish statistical significance (p=0.25 for GL versus EMA). The stronger suppression achieved with fractional memory is accompanied by greater disruption of retained and general factual knowledge, suggesting a shift in model behavior rather than more selective forgetting. Whether the targeted information becomes genuinely inaccessible rather than merely less likely to be reproduced remains unresolved.</jats:p>
title: Valence-Aware Gradient Memory and Fractional Kernel Comparisons for LoRA-Based Language Model Unlearning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents operating on long-running tasks inevitably exceed their usable context window, forcing a choice about what history to discard. In practice, most agent frameworks default to one of two simple strategies: dropping the oldest turns, or replacing them with an LLM-generated summary. A third strategy, retrieving only the turns most relevant to the current query regardless of age, is common in retrieval-augmented systems but is rarely compared head-to-head against the first two under a controlled, fact-recall task. We introduce a synthetic long-context recall task in which specific facts (random codes, names, dates) are planted at known positions within a long sequence of conversational turns, and an agent must answer questions about both early-planted and recently-planted facts after its context has been compressed to a fixed budget. We compare three context-management strategies: dropoldest, summarize-oldest, and keep-most-relevant, using real calls to a production LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6), grading each answer automatically against a known gold value. Across 20 independent trials (360 graded queries), summarize-oldest achieves 94.2% overall recall accuracy, keep-most-relevant achieves 60.0%, and drop-oldest achieves only 41.7% (χ 2 = 75.17, p &lt; 0.00001). The effect is driven almost entirely by facts stated early in the conversation: drop-oldest recalls 0% of early-stated facts (Fisher's exact test vs. both alternatives, p &lt; 0.00001), confirming that its failures are not occasional misses but a complete, systematic loss of any information outside the retained recency window. Summarize-oldest retains 90.4% accuracy on these same early facts despite paying only one additional LLM call per compression event, while keep-most-relevant, using a deliberately weak, local, non-semantic embedding, partially but incompletely recovers early facts (61.5%). We discuss the practical implications for agent framework design and the limitations of our synthetic, single-model, single-budget setup.</jats:p>
title: An Empirical Evaluation of Context-Management Strategies for Large Language Model Agents Under Forced Context Compression

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) commonly employ key–value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states during autoregressive inference. However, its measured performance benefit depends on workload characteristics and the memory environment. This study presents a controlled systems characterization of KV-cache performance across input context length, grouped-query attention configurations, and GPU-memory residency. Experiments use Qwen2.5-3B and SmolLM3-3B under verified fully resident conditions with fixed 128-token generation, prompt lengths from 128 to 2048 tokens, randomized cache-enabled/cache-disabled execution, GPU telemetry, and repeated paired validation. KV-cache speedup increases from 1.34× to 8.31× for Qwen2.5-3B and from 1.28× to 8.62× for SmolLM3-3B. At 2048 prompt tokens, 30 randomized paired trials confirm mean speedups of 8.10× and 8.51×, corresponding to runtime reductions of 87.65% and 88.25%, while physical GPU-memory utilization remains below 61%. Despite SmolLM3-3B requiring twice the theoretical KV-cache storage per token, both models show comparable context-dependent scaling in the fully resident regime. A separate Mistral-7B case study further demonstrates that memory pressure can substantially alter apparent speedup. These results establish KV-cache speedup as workload- and system-dependent and demonstrate that meaningful benchmarking requires reporting context length, cache configuration, model and cache footprints, physical accelerator-memory residency, runtime, throughput, and relevant GPU-memory conditions during each inference experiment.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The growing demands on memory and contextual processing within expansive language models present critical challenges, particularly in resource efficiency and scalability across diverse linguistic tasks. Introducing a novel framework, Dynamic Contextual Scope Management (DCSM), this approach significantly redefines adaptive memory reallocation, equipping language models with a refined mechanism to allocate and segment memory based on dynamic context relevance. By realigning memory allocation in real-time to maintain only pertinent information, the DCSM framework achieves substantial improvements in memory usage, response coherence, and overall model adaptability. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's impact, with DCSM-enhanced models demonstrating up to 33.6% reductions in memory consumption and notable enhancements in response accuracy, latency, and computational efficiency. The integration of DCSM within large-scale language models not only addresses longstanding limitations in handling extended contexts but also establishes a scalable pathway for adaptive, high-performance language processing. These findings highlight DCSM's potential for transformative applications in contexts requiring efficient handling of extensive and evolving information, fostering a new standard for adaptive memory systems in the field of advanced language models.</jats:p>
title: Dynamic Contextual Scope Management: A Novel Framework for Adaptive Memory Reallocation in Large Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Abstract: High throughput serving of large language models (LLMs) requires batching sufficiently many requests at a time. However, existing systems struggle because the key-value cache (KV cache) memory for each request is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically. When managed inefficiently, this memory can be significantly wasted by fragmentation and redundant duplication, limiting the batch size. To address this problem we proposed a Paged Attention. An alternative algorithm inspired by the classical virtual memory and paging techniques in operating systems. An LLM serving system that achieves (1) near-zero waste in KV cache memory and (2) flexible sharing of KV cache within and across requests to further reduce memory usage. Our evaluations show that LLM improves the throughput of popular LLMs by 2-4× with the same level of latency compared to the state-of-the-art systems, such as Faster Transformer and Orca. The improvement is more pronounced with longer sequences, larger models, and more complex decoding algorithms</jats:p>
title: Open-AI model Efficient Memory Reduce Management for the Large Language Models (LLMs) Serving with Paged Attention of sharing the KV Cashes

items.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as clinical decision support tools in healthcare, yet the impact of query language on their performance remains unclear, particularly in specialized domains like dental traumatology. This study evaluated whether LLM performance in dental trauma management differs based on the language of clinical scenarios (English vs. Turkish) and compared performance across three AI models. Methods Twenty-seven clinical scenarios covering 13 dental trauma categories were presented to ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3.0, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet in both English and Turkish, generating 162 responses. Two blinded endodontists independently evaluated responses using a standardized rubric assessing accuracy (40%), completeness (35%), and safety (25%) against IADT 2020 Guidelines. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Language effects were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; model comparisons employed Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction. Results Inter-rater reliability was good across all dimensions (ICC: 0.738–0.836). ChatGPT showed the strongest language effect with 9.14% higher performance in English (p < 0.001, r = 0.874). Gemini showed moderate English advantage (5.69%, p = 0.003, r = 0.572). Claude exhibited language independence with virtually identical performance in both languages (-0.02%, p = 0.220). In English, significant model differences emerged (H = 22.31, p < 0.001); however, model performance converged in Turkish (H = 2.89, p = 0.236). Conclusions Language-dependent performance variations in LLMs are model-specific rather than universal. While ChatGPT achieved highest absolute scores, Claude’s language independence may offer more reliable performance in non-English clinical settings. These findings have implications for deployment of AI in multilingual healthcare environments.
title: Impact of Query Language on Large Language Model Performance in Dental Trauma Management: A Comparative Evaluation of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are inherently limited in processing long contexts by their inability to handle sequences longer than tens of thousands of tokens due to the quadratic complexity of full self-attention, and by the lack of reasoning fidelity in current approximations. We introduce CLEAR (Compressed Long-context Efficient Adaptive Reasoning), a unified framework to tackle this trilemma in a three-pronged way: a Hierarchical Token Compressor (HTC) that builds multi-granularity token pyramids by importance-weighted pooling to reduce the effective sequence length by up to 4x – 16x without compromising the semantic fidelity; a Sparse Attention Orchestrator (SAO) that adaptively routes attention computation across local, strided, and global patterns using learned routing weights; and a Dynamic Memory Controller (DMC) that manages a selective KV-cache with relevance-scored eviction and retrieval policies. We establish four theoretical contributions: an \(\:O\left(n\text{l}\text{o}\text{g}n\right)\) complexity reduction over quadratic attention, an information preservation bound for hierarchical compression, an \(\:{\mathcal{l}}_{{\infty\:}}\) approximation error bound for sparse attention outputs, and a regret bound for online KV-cache management. Empirically, CLEAR achieves state-of-the-art results on SCROLLS (67.3), LongBench (63.8), L-Eval (71.4), and NeedleBench (94.2%), delivering \(\:3.2\times\:\) throughput improvement and \(\:4.7\times\:\) memory reduction over full-attention baselines at 32K context length, with less than 1.2% accuracy degradation.
title: Efficient Long-Context Reasoning in Large Language Models: Hierarchical Token Compression with Sparse Attention and Dynamic Memory Management

items.abstract: The prevalence of diabetes is rapidly increasing in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), making it one of the fastest-growing global health emergencies of the modern era. Despite efforts by healthcare practitioners, the government, and communities to minimise the associated complications and mortality, there are significant challenges that can be potentially alleviated through innovative digital health technologies. This study developed a domain-specific large language model (DS-LLM) aimed at improving diabetes care and management using a case study of South Africa. To achieve this, local data was collected and supplemented with benchmark and medical Hugging Face datasets. Medical pre-trained large language models (LLMs): BioMedLM (2.7B) and BioMistral-7B were selected as base models, along with Qwen3-8B (a non-specialised LLM). Two Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques: prompt tuning and Quantised Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) were applied, with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applied on the best-performing LLM. The fine-tuned LLMs were evaluated by comparing their respective performance with Diabetica-7B , a specialised diabetes LLM. The final dataset comprised 18,079 processed question-answer pairs (14% artificially generated for the South African context) and 1,596 documents, covering medication, management, diagnosis, screening, and general diabetes topics that pertain to South Africa. For fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice questions formats, Qwen QLoRA outperformed all LLMs (ROUGE-1 = 0.793, ROUGE-L= 0.792, and BERTScore F1 = 0.940). Diabetica had the highest BLEU score (0.465), while Qwen3-8B had 0.365. For multiple-choice questions only, Qwen3-8B QLoRA achieved a top accuracy of 80.7%. For short and long answers, BioMistral-7B QLoRA performed slightly better, with all models scoring above 0.800. These findings highlight the promising use of LLMs for diabetes care.
title: A Domain-specific Large Language Model for Diabetes Care and Management

items.abstract: <jats:p>Mandatory job rotations are a cornerstone of the Malaysian civil service, designed to enhance governance, reduce integrity risks, and foster organizational agility. However, these rotations present significant onboarding challenges, requiring employees to rapidly adapt to diverse roles and complex responsibilities, particularly in 'hot seat' and high-risk-to-corruption positions. This study focuses on the Jabatan Kastam Diraja Malaysia (JKDM), where the need for efficient onboarding is heightened by the structured tenure of job rotations. The necessity to quickly acclimate to new roles within a defined period, especially in sensitive positions, underscores the urgency of effective onboarding strategies. To address the inherent onboarding complexities, particularly in navigating intricate customs regulations, this research proposes leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), with a specific focus on NotebookLM. NotebookLM's ability to ingest and summarize extensive regulatory documents, coupled with features like interactive training modules and AI-powered Q&A, offers a dynamic, personalized learning experience. This approach aims to surpass traditional training limitations, streamlining onboarding, enhancing knowledge transfer, and boosting productivity within JKDM. The study outlines an implementation plan, including a pilot program and department-wide rollout, with expected outcomes of improved onboarding efficiency, enhanced knowledge sharing, and increased operational effectiveness, ultimately contributing to a more agile and integrity-driven public service.</jats:p>
title: ENHANCING JOB ROTATION ONBOARDING IN THE MALAYSIAN PUBLIC SECTOR: A NotebookLM Large Language Model Case Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>The deployment of large language models (LLMs) at long context lengths is increasingly limited by memory rather than compute. During autoregressive decoding, the key-value (KV) cache stores the key and value activations of processed tokens, grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, and must often be streamed for each generated token. In long-context and high-throughput settings, this makes decoding memory-bandwidthbound and exposes the memory wall. This survey gives a unified, hardware-aware treatment of techniques that mitigate this bottleneck. We formalise it through the roofline model and a VRAM-footprint analysis separating compute-bound prefill from memorybound decoding, then organise the literature into four complementary layers: algorithmic compression (quantization, eviction and sparsification, and token, low-rank, or learned merging); architectural redesign (multi-query and grouped-query attention, low-rank latent attention, and recurrent or hybrid state-space models); system-level management (paged memory, prefix sharing, cross-request transport, and tiered offloading); and hardware acceleration (decoding kernels, fusion, and processing-in-memory). For each we give the governing mechanism, achievable memory reduction, and accuracy-latency trade-offs. Distinct from prior surveys, we (a) unify the four layers under a co-design and Pareto-frontier framework, (b) consolidate the evidence on multi-tenant KV cache security and side-channel leakage, and (c) analyse cache degradation in long-horizon agentic loops. To make this gap actionable, we propose Matched-Budget Evaluation (MBE), a lightweight reporting protocol and accompanying pilot harness for describing KV-cache results at fixed memory budgets. We present MBE as a standardization proposal, not a fully validated benchmark. It targets researchers and engineers combining KV cache optimisations under deployment constraints.</jats:p>
title: Breaking the Memory Wall: A Survey of Key-Value (KV) Cache Compression for Efficient Large Language Model (LLM) Inference&nbsp;

<jats:p>This research incorporates artificial intelligence (AI) into asset integrity and process safety (AIPS) management, aiming
to revolutionize conventional methods. It facilitates the automation of risk assessments, enhances predictive analytics,
and supports the development of proactive measures to mitigate potential incidents. It explores the application of a
generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) based large language models (LLM) to analyse and classify AIPS indicators
from vast datasets to generate actionable recommendations to prevent future incidents. A comparative study between
two onshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants; one utilizing AI-driven AIPS management and the other relying on
manual data analysis is presented. The results indicate that AI-driven approaches significantly enhance the accuracy
and speed of incident classifications, reducing data processing times. The test model effectively predicts potential
future failures by analysing past incident patterns, enabling informed decision-making to prevent and mitigate future
failures. The findings highlight the importance of adopting AI-driven AIPS management as a standard practice. It also
emphasises the need for stronger collaboration between academia and industry in AI solutions to drive technological
advancements for sustainability.</jats:p>
title: An Industrial Application of a Large Language Model to Enhancing Asset Integrity and Process Safety Management

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive review of Memory-Augmented Large Language Models (LLMs), with a particular emphasis on optimization strategies and alignment with human preferences. We synthesize recent advances in memory-efficient training, model compression (quantization, pruning, low-rank approximations, and differentiable SVD), and architectural innovations that integrate explicit memory modules to enhance long-context reasoning and interpretability. The paper also examines alignment methodologies, ranging from supervised fine-tuning to reinforcement learning with human or AI feedback, as well as emerging approaches for inference-time personalization. Beyond technical optimization, we highlight challenges in evaluation, data efficiency, and ethical considerations such as fairness, privacy, and memorization risks. Representative applications in domains including business, healthcare, education, and scientific discovery illustrate the practical value and limitations of optimized and memory-augmented LLMs. Our contributions are threefold: (i) providing a structured overview of the state of the art in LLM optimization, memory augmentation, and alignment, (ii) identifying open challenges in efficiency, interpretability, and responsible deployment, and (iii) outlining future research directions toward more scalable, trustworthy, and user-centric LLMs. This review offers researchers and practitioners a timely roadmap for advancing the next generation of large-scale language models.</jats:p>
title: From Memory to Alignment: A Comprehensive Review of Large Language Model Optimization

items.abstract: <jats:p>A moving permanent magnet induces currents in nearby conductors and superconducting loops. This electrodynamic back-action produces forces that are history-dependent and, in general, cannot be represented by a conservative potential depending only on instantaneous separation. We derive a compact state--space model for the axial motion of a magnetic dipole coupled to an $N$-turn loop with inductance $L$ and resistance $R$. Using Faraday's law for the flux linkage $\Lambda(x)=N\Phi(x)$, the coupled dynamics are \[ L\dot i + R i = -\Lambda'(x)\dot x,\qquad F_{\mathrm{em}}(t)= i(t)\,\Lambda'(x(t)), \] which defines a passive, causal magnetomechanical memory element. Linearizing about an operating point $x_0$ yields an exact complex dynamic stiffness \[ K_{\mathrm{em}}(\omega) \equiv -\frac{F_{\mathrm{em}}(\omega)}{X(\omega)} = \frac{\Lambda'(x_0)^2\, i\omega}{R+i\omega L} = k_\infty\,\frac{i\omega\tau}{1+i\omega\tau}, \quad k_\infty=\frac{\Lambda'(x_0)^2}{L},\ \tau=\frac{L}{R}. \] We show that this back-action is exactly equivalent to a mechanical Maxwell element, derive closed-form expressions for added stiffness and added damping, and provide direct identification formulas for $(\tau,k_\infty)$ from measured complex stiffness. The dipole--loop geometry further admits an analytic design rule: the coupling gradient $|\Lambda'(x_0)|$ is maximized at $x_0=a/2$ where $a$ is the loop radius. Finally, we connect commonly proposed \emph{jerk-like} and \emph{absement-like} terms to controlled low- and high-frequency asymptotic expansions of the same passive kernel (with explicit validity limits). All predictions are validated by reproducible Python simulations, and code to generate figures and data is provided.</jats:p>
title: Electromagnetic Back-Action in Dipole–Loop Magnetomechanics: State–Space Model, Memory Kernel, and Jerk/Absement Asymptotes

items.abstract: <jats:p>Current memory augmentation approaches for Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), inject retrieved content by concatenating it to the input prompt. This paradigm consumes valuable context window tokens and requires careful prompt engineering. We propose Dynamic KV Injection (DKI), a training-free, inference-time user-level cross-session memory system that injects Key-Value representations directly into the attention mechanism without consuming prompt tokens. Scope Definition: DKI is designed specifically for user-level memory (personal preferences, session history, user context), not for external knowledge bases or public data retrieval. This focused scope enables architectural simplifications and reduces position encoding risks. Our key contributions include: (1) a paradigm shift from token-level to attention-level memory injection; (2) Memory Influence Scaling (MIS) with continuous strength control α ∈ [0, 1]; (3) Query-Conditioned Memory Projection using FiLM-style modulation; (4) Dual-Factor Gating combining uncertainty and relevance signals; (5) Hybrid Injection Strategy: negative-position K/V injection for stable preferences + suffix-prompt injection (explicit token-level history reference) for dynamic session history; and (6) Standardized Plugin Architecture enabling configuration-based deployment. We introduce the Attention Budget Reallocation Hypothesis: in reasoning-intensive tasks, the marginal benefit of releasing token budget exceeds the marginal cost of increased attention computation. Preliminary experiments on PersonaChat (n=500) show comparable memory recall (86.2% vs 87.3%) with 43.7% reduction in subsequent-turn latency; DKI significantly outperforms RAG by +10-16% at user context lengths >2500 tokens, strongly supporting the budget reallocation hypothesis.</jats:p>
title: Dynamic KV Injection: An Attention-Level User Memory System for Large Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent yet factually incorrect statements—a failure that mirrors false memory in biological systems. Whether such errors arise from causally identifiable and manipulable circuit elements has remained unknown. Here we adapt the engram framework from systems neuroscience and combine causal mediation analysis with a double-dissociation logic to localize, verify, and rewrite factual and false memory traces in GPT-style transformers. We discover that sparse sets of knowledge neurons—canonical ensembles of approximately 8–15 units—function as memory engrams: silencing them selectively erases target-fact retrieval while matched controls remain intact; exogenous activation forces the fact into output even under neutral prompts. Rigorous controls, including patterned activation and non-engram amplification, confirm identity-specific sufficiency. Critically, counterfactual fine-tuning creates false memory engrams that deviate geometrically toward lexical co-occurrence subspaces; formal mediation analysis reveals that this geometric corruption causally mediates 65% of the pathway from falsity to erroneous output. Exploiting this divergence, we construct an unsupervised Memory Credibility Score that predicts hallucination propensity without behavioural testing, generalizing across relations and model scales. The framework extends to multi-hop and temporal reasoning and enables reversible, context-dependent memory control unavailable to permanent weight-editing methods. Our findings establish a causal sufficiency-and-necessity account of factual retrieval, diagnose representational pathologies underlying hallucination, and deliver a precision toolkit for understanding and certifying knowledge in LLMs.</jats:p>
title: Causal Engram Circuits for Factual and Hallucinated Memory in Large Language Models

items.abstract:
BACKGROUND

There is a gap for at least 10,000 endocrinologists, which might cause delayed treatment in some patients with DKA. The efficacy of large language model (LLM) in improving productivity has been illustrated in rehabilitation medicine. However, it remains unclear in the management for patients with DKA.

 OBJECTIVE

This study aimed to investigate the application potentials of large language model in the management of patients with diabetes ketoacidosis (DKA).

 METHODS

ChatGPT-4 was applied to generate information of diagnosis, treatment and regular follow-up based on a classic DKA case. Junior and senior endocrinologist were invited to review accuracy and limitations of the output to determine the rough value of ChatGPT-4 in the routine practice, especially in DKA.

 RESULTS

ChatGPT-4 could respond in seconds and generated information including the diagnosis, regimen and follow-up pertinent to the case. Also, it provided rationale for the diagnosis or suggestion outputted. Compared with the standard answer or guideline, recommendation ChatGPT-4 offered was more elaborate, which including self-management education, diet and exercise, assessment for chronic disease management follow-up, and psychosocial support. However, there were some limitations, including the inability to provide the most suitable recommendations in the complex situations. Similar findings were found when compared with the endocrinologists.

 CONCLUSIONS

Large language model present tremulous potentials in facilitating routine practice and medical education on improving the working efficiency of endocrinologists.
title: The Application Potential of Large Language Model in the Management for Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Systematic Review (Preprint)

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous tools across numerous domains such as education, healthcare, and professional advisory services. However, their susceptibility to sycophancy-a bias toward echoing user prompts over independently reasoning-poses a critical threat to model reliability. We present a Bayesian-latent variable framework that introduces a hidden sycophancy score Si,m,u,p ∼ N (0, σ 2 S) to quantify such behavior. The framework defines a flip indicator ∆i,m,u,p ∈ {−1, 0, +1} to distinguish regressive (accuracydecreasing) from progressive (accuracy-increasing) shifts. Our generative logistic model ties correctness probabilities to latent agreement pressure via Pr(ŷ (1) = 1) = σ(x ⊤ β + γmSi,m,u,p), enabling rigorous posterior inference. Empirically, we find an average sycophancy-induced shift of E[|S|] ≈ 0.8σS, and a model susceptibility factor γ that directly controls response volatility. Simulated results show that nearly 50% of responses flip under user cues, with regressive flips dominating when γ < 0.    Our approach provides a statistically grounded diagnostic for  auditing and improving trustworthiness in LLM behavior under  social influence. Simulation code for this study is available at:  https://github.com/ParthaPRay/Sycophancy_in_LLM_model.</jats:p>

items.abstract: In the seismic impedance inversion, the low-frequency information reflects the general trend of the impedance curve. Without low-frequency information, inversion results can not accurately reflect stratigraphic changes. Seismic data are also spatially correlated, while the conventional inversion methods do not consider the spatial correlation of geological structures, which may lead to poor lateral continuity of the inversion results. To alleviate these problems, we proposes a low-frequency constrained seismic impedance inversion method combining Large Kernel Attention (LKA) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). Our network structure is divided into an inversion module and a low-frequency feature extraction module. In the inversion module, we integrate LKA and LSTM into the network, which can improve the lateral continuity of the inversion results. The low-frequency feature extraction module constrains the entire network structure and extract more refined low-frequency features. To demonstrate the reliability of the proposed method, we applied it to the SEAM model. Experiments show that our method has the best lateral continuity and accuracy, with Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Coefficient of Determination (\(R^{2}\)) of 0.0485 and 0.9164, respectively, as well as strong noise immunity. This method also achieves favorable inversion results on the Volve field seismic data.
title: Low-Frequency Constrained Seismic Impedance Inversion Combining Large Kernel Attention and Long Short-Term Memory
